title: Stream-priority queueing trace - Nsight timeline analysis (Nov 2026)
content:
Summary:

This is a working note from a focused Nsight timeline session investigating unexpected stalls and uneven SM utilization when using CUDA Graph replay with multiple streams and varying stream priorities. High-level finding: small, frequent kernel launches from low-priority worker streams can preempt high-priority inference streams indirectly via internal driver/queueing effects, producing sporadic latency spikes and lower-than-expected occupancy on the main inference kernels.

Why we ran this:
- Customer P99 spikes during high-concurrency burst tests despite stable average throughput.
- Microbenchmarks with isolated kernel runs show good throughput, but integrated Nsight traces show stalling and underutilized SMs in production-like runs.

Experiment setup (short):
- Machine: p4d-like baseline (A100-equivalent), 8 GPUs test node (we ran single-GPU traces).
- Driver / CUDA: NVIDIA driver 535.xx, CUDA 12.2 in runtime image (repro images in PR linked above).
- Model: trimmed GPT-style transformer for inference path (seq_len 512, kv-cache enabled, beam=1).
- Serving runtime config: cudaGraph capture per-request, persistent worker pool, per-request streams for postprocessing (tokenization/IO), main inference stream (high priority).
- Nsight config: timeline capture 20s, API tracing (kernel names, API calls), NVTX markers inserted at: request-enter, capture-start, capture-end, graph-launch, kv-load-start, kv-load-end.
- Workload: 1200 qps synthetic client with Poisson arrival; mixed short/long sequences to reproduce bursts.

Repro steps (condensed):
1) Start node with runtime built from PR/842 image.
2) Enable full Nsight CLI capture: nsight-sys --trace=nvtx,cuda --output=trace.qdrep --duration=20s --capture-mode=manual
3) Run synthetic client (profiles attached in linked artifacts).
4) Collect trace, open in Nsight Systems.

Observations from timeline:
- Graph-launch vs kernel-start gap: For many requests we observed a 200-500us gap between cudaGraphLaunch API and the first kernel execution. Gaps concentrated when multiple background worker streams are active.
- Stream contention pattern: Low-priority worker streams issue many tiny kernels (memcpy, elementwise ops for preprocessing) that show up as many short (~10-30us) kernels. These create intermittent bursts of PCIe/SM command consumption visible as thin red bands in timeline that align with P99 latency spikes.
- Preemption-like behavior: Although the high-priority stream keeps being scheduled first, the driver/queue submission causes short stalls (incoming command queue depth drops) resulting in kernel dispatch gaps; NSIGHT shows scheduling stalls annotated as "queue wait" adjacent to the main kernels.
- Occupancy vs achieved SMs: Main attention kernels report theoretical occupancy 72% but achieved SM active cycles are 48-60% during burst windows. Exported counters: active_warps_per_sm avg=19.3, max=31; theoretical max warps/sm=64 for the kernel config.
- KV cache load overlap: KV cache memcopies scheduled on separate streams overlapped with main kernel execution; when KV copy proceeded on the same GPU FIFO (same engine) it caused occasional serialization and stalls.

Numbers (representative slices):
- Typical main attention kernel time (isolated): 1.9ms.
- Main kernel time (integrated burst window): 2.35ms (includes 200-500us pre-dispatch gap).
- Small preprocessing kernels: 10-35us each, 200-600 of them per second per worker stream.
- Measured SM occupancy (nsys counters): theoretical 72%, achieved 52% median, drops to 38% during spikes.

Hypothesis / root cause candidates: 
1) Stream priority alone doesn't guarantee immediate isolation: driver-level command merging and engine contention reduce isolation when many small kernels flood low-priority streams.
2) CUDA Graph capture + replay introduces a gap between launch and kernel execution in presence of concurrent stream submissions (graph node scheduling costs + driver serialization).
3) KV cache memcpy patterns (non-pinned buffers, synchronous calls) amplify serialization; pinned+async copies or using GPUDirect may mitigate.

Short experiments we ran to validate hypotheses:
- Disabled worker stream kernels -> trace gaps disappear, occupancy rises to expected levels. Latency stabilizes.
- Raised worker stream priority to medium -> reduced gaps but overall latencies of worker tasks increased (bad for throughput).
- Merged multiple tiny preproc kernels into batched kernels (local micro-optimization) -> drastically fewer small kernels, driver load lowered, main kernel gaps reduced.
- Changed KV memcpy to cudaMemcpyAsync with dedicated copy stream + cudaStreamWaitEvent before main kernel -> improved overlap and reduced serialization events.

Actionable mitigations (short-term):
- Introduce batching for preprocessing on worker streams to reduce kernel count per request. Prefer fused elementwise kernels instead of many small ops.
- Make KV cache copies explicitly asynchronous and use pinned staging buffers for host->device paths. Add a dedicated DMA/transfer stream with higher priority than background worker streams (but lower than main inference stream) and ensure graphs wait on the copy completion with events.
- Adjust stream priorities: main inference stream = 100, dma stream = 80, worker preprocess streams = 60 (priority scale is relative; tune experimentally).
- Investigate limiting per-GPU outstanding kernel launches from worker threadpool (token-bucket) to keep driver queue depth reasonable.

Longer-term / architectural changes to consider: 
- Move ephemeral preprocessing off-GPU for very small ops (CPU vectorized path) to avoid flood of micro-kernels. Benchmark cost tradeoffs.
- Use persistent kernels or fused operator kernels that reduce kernel launch rate for attention/postprocessing patterns.
- Rework capture granularity: capture larger composite graphs that include preproc + inference so the driver treats the entire flow as fewer graph nodes. Must weigh memory usage and capture overhead.

Open questions and next steps (todo list):
- [ ] Run controlled experiments to sweep stream priority values and record P50/P95/P99 and SM utilization. Assign: Daniel. Target: 2026-11-25.
- [ ] Add a microbenchmark that floods with small kernels (configurable size/frequency) to measure threshold where queueing impacts begin. Assign: Ethan. Target: 2026-11-22.
- [ ] Instrument runtime to record per-request small-kernel counts and average sizes (telemetry). Add minimal NVTX markers around worker kernels for aggregated traces. Assign: Marina.
- [ ] Test pinned buffer pipeline for KV cache copies in staging branch. Compare host->device transfer time and driver serialization. Assign: Aisha.

Notes / loose ideas (brain dump):
- For multitenant nodes, consider reserving a small portion of SMs (or separate GPU partitions if hardware supports MIG) for high-priority inference to avoid interference from background tasks.
- Check whether the driver version has known issues with stream priority enforcement; test with 535 vs 545 drivers.
- When using GPU coalescing features (cuBLAS/cuDNN heuristics), small kernel flood can defeat heuristics and cause worse-than-expected paths.

Files & traces attached in linked artifacts. Trace snippets to highlight when reviewing:
- nvtx-range [graph-launch] -> gap -> kernel-start timeline slices (these are the clearest indicators).
- "queue wait" markers and API call timings grouped by stream id.

Conclusions (working):
- Root cause appears to be a combination of small-kernel flooding on low-priority streams + driver-level queue serialization that introduces gaps ahead of main kernels launched via CUDA Graph. Occupancy impact is real: achieved SM cycles fall significantly during bursts.
- Practical immediate wins: reduce kernel launch rate from background preprocess, make DMA async with pinned buffers, and tune stream priorities + limit outstanding worker submissions.

If we can validate these fixes in the short experiments, we should roll a staging change that implements kernel batching + async KV staging and then run a 24-hour soak with the synthetic burst workload. If that stabilizes P99 and occupancy metrics we can prepare a short engineering note for product/CS for customers facing similar P99 spikes.

-- Aisha
